The words

Father of all our mercies, thou
In whom we move and live,
Hear us in heaven, thy dwelling, now,
And answer, and forgive.

When, harassed by ten thousand foes,
Our helplessness we feel,
O, give the weary soul repose,
The wounded spirit heal.

When dire temptations gather round
And threaten or allure,
By storm or calm, in thee be found
A refuge strong and sure.

When age advances, may we grow
In faith, in hope, and love,
And walk in holiness below
To holiness above.

When earthly joys and cares depart,
Desire and envy cease,
Be thou the portion of our heart, —
In thee may we have peace.

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum D and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on d (D), on the first syllable of “Father”, as a pickup before the first full bar.
  • Count the time. 4/4 means four crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

James Montgomery wrote these words. They were printed in Hymns for Christian Devotion, compiled by John G. Adams and Edwin H. Chapin (Boston, 1846), as hymn 470 of its twenty-second edition (1853), “Prayer for Grace in Trial”.

The book printed the words without tunes, marked Common Metre (8.6.8.6), to be sung to any tune of that metre. This page sets them to CAITHNESS; any other Common Metre tune fits them as well.

  • Words: James Montgomery (1771–1854)
  • Melody (1635): Scottish Psalter

Questions about Father of All Our Mercies, Thou

What is the doh of Father of All Our Mercies, Thou?

In this version, in D major, doh is D. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does Father of All Our Mercies, Thou start on?

It starts on d (D in D major), a pickup on the first syllable of “Father” before the first full bar. Find doh first, then sing up or down to d.

Is Father of All Our Mercies, Thou in the public domain?

Yes. James Montgomery died in 1854; the words were in print by 1853 and the music in 1635. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
